newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi mobilised for two million haj pilgrims.
newsitem.headline: Saudi mobilised for two million haj pilgrims.

text.p: Up to two million Moslems in seamless white robes are converging on the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia to perform the haj pilgrimage, a centuries-old rite which reaches its climax on April 16.

More than 37,000 doctors, nurses, security men, bakers, cleaners and garbage collectors have been recruited to service the pilgrims -- half of whom have been arriving in the desert kingdom over the last few weeks from around 100 countries.
The haj is one of the five pillars of Islam and each Moslem who can afford it should perform it at least once.
Preparations for the biggest gathering of Moslems are almost completed. By Wednesday 980,000 pilgrims had arrived in Saudi Arabia by air, land and sea, immigration officials said.
Of the two million pilgrims, one million would travel to Mecca from other parts of the kingdom under a quota system.
Saudi newspapers said planes carrying pilgrims were landing at the rate of one a minute at Jeddah airport on Wednesday, two days before the deadline for pilgrims to arrive for haj.
Officials said half a million pilgrims had been vaccinated against meningitis over the past few days.
Maintaining security and safety is a main concern.

At least 15,000 security men are patrolling Mecca and roads leading to it to ensure peace. Cameras installed on main roads, bridges and tunnels monitor pilgrims' movements to ensure that haj, in the past marked by tragedy, proceeds peacefully.
Up to 270 pilgrims were killed in a stampede in 1994.
Saudi officials have urged the pilgrims to abide by security instructions especially in usually congested areas.

Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent 70 billion riyals ($18.6 billion) on expanding sites in Mecca, including the Grand Mosque housing Kaaba, a black cube-shaped building covered by gold-embroidered black silk that Moslems across the world face to pray.
Saudi television has been showing pilgrims -- men wrapped in two simple white sheets and women in long white or black robes and headscarves-- circling Kaaba on foot.

Saudi Interior Minister Prince Nayef urged all pilgrims to repect the religious ritual, including Iranians whose country insists on holding political rallies during haj every year denouncing the United States and Israel.
The staging of the rallies had since 1987 -- when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes -- escalated tensions between Saudi Arabia and its powerful neighbour Iran.
But this year Iranian officials, trying to improve ties with the kingdom and other Gulf Arab states, have been using softer tones towards Riyadh even when calling for the rallies.

"Iranian officials understand the matter and heed should be taken from the previous years," Prince Nayef said. "We hope that all pilgrims, not only the Iranians, will respect this sacred ritual and respect its security and the security" of Saudi.
Riyadh has repeatedly said it would deal harshly with pilgrims who defy its ban on political activity and Prince Nayef said he did not believe rallies would take place this year.

In another controversy surrounding haj, the kingdom on Wednesday allowed an Iraqi plane carrying 104 pilgrims to land in Jeddah, in defiance of U.N. sanctions. Iraq had the day before sent pilgrims by road for the first time since 1994.
Prince Nayef said the Iraqi plane was allowed to enter the kingdom after authorities were told it carried Iraqi pilgrims.
Since 1995 Saudi Arabia has allowed three Libyan planes to fly pilgrims to Jeddah in defiance of U.N. sanctions.

The kingdom said the first day of haj would be on April 15 when pilgrims pray at the Grand Mosque. On the same day and on April 16, 13,000 buses will take them to Mount Arafat, where Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago.
Some will walk the 11 km (seven miles). "I have answered your call, God. There is no God but you," they will pray at Mount Arafat, marking the climax of haj.

They will then spend the night in tents in Mena, where they will stone three monuments representing the devil. On April 17 they head back for prayers in Mecca, marking the first day of Eid al-Adha (the Feast of Sacrifice) when Moslems around the world slaughter animals and donate them to the poor.
Saudi officials said 500,000 sheep and 15,000 head of cattle and camels will be sacrificed by pilgrims this year.
